title: ❄️ Tharvorn — Second Age Winter, Maritime & Highland Histories
rawNotionMarkup: Tharvorn, Second Age Years 1–1,437 in Avarran retrospective dating. Tharvorn's own era names and internal calendar boundaries are not yet established. The date bands below allow cross-continental comparison; they do not impose the Avarran names Awakening, Wonder or Fire on Tharvorn's people. This is new creator-authorized, revisable regional history. ## A coast where old light could no longer be trusted (Years 1–115) Tharvorn's fjord dwellings, upland halls, forest villages and storm coasts did not experience the post-Cataclysm world equally. A ward protecting a boathouse might work on one night and fail on the next. In the First Salt-Winter, a succession of local storms and delayed fish runs brought hunger to several independently governed coast communities. The name is retrospective and refers to regional weather and supply breakdowns, not an extra planetwide moon-shattering event. Some lords requisitioned boats and forbade independent fishers from landing catch; a few villages divided stores by household need, sometimes against their governors' orders. Among the first efforts at ordinary, verifiable rescue were the Cedar-Peg Routes, a system of carved wooden storm markers, stepped cairns and manually maintained shelters. Wolvenkin trail families, Bearfolk caravan houses, Troll river builders, human boatmen, some Giants and cliff-dwelling Harpies all participated in different places. Not all were allies, and certain local chiefs regarded rescue corridors as unauthorized passage over their land. One northern town hanged a guide for sheltering travelers without charging an official winter toll. His sister, Mava Stone-Lantern, later helped organize the Gate-Side Table, where decisions about shelter duty were recorded publicly. ### The Four Smoke Lodges Several unrelated forest and highland settlements negotiated a practical Four Smoke Agreement: each lodge would maintain a physical smoke beacon, a winter store, a messenger route and a spare shelter key, rather than trust a single protection spell. One participating Giant household offered enormous roof timbers but demanded rights over nearby quarry access; some smallfolk councils considered the price exploitative and found other builders. The resulting compromise made timber a paid trade rather than a hereditary tribute. This was no universal Giant–Human treaty and no origin charter for the modern Northern Holds. ## The reign of thaw and debt (Years 116–321) The coastal lordship of Veskhar Reach, a narrow collection of ports and neighboring farms rather than all Tharvorn, grew rich by granting privileged whaling, fishing and saltwork licenses. Its ambitious Lady Haldra of the Quays funded stone breakwaters and nonmagical navigation lights; she also allowed lenders to seize the working boats of families with unpaid winter debts. Her own court records portrayed her as a savior, while harbor workers remembered the Winter of Locked Oars, when boats sat idle as hunger spread. A guild of boat repairers, led in part by Jorven Ash-Wake, an elderly human master, and Urrek Flintfoot, a Troll timber fitter, refused to repair seized ships without written release of their crews. Guards assaulted them; some were imprisoned. The strike produced the Three-Bell Settlement, a limited harbor rule permitting independent review of seizure after storms. The new rule did not erase old suffering or end debt bondage everywhere. Children of imprisoned workers later became respected pilots and union-minded shipwrights, not simply inherited victims. On the forest margins, Troll families retained distinct rites around river crossings, and Bearfolk lodges debated whether food stores should be shared with neighboring villages. Some Foxfolk traders were prized for fair winter contracts; others exploited isolation. Forest keepers from Eldar, Ent and smaller woodland communities fought over whether a dangerous path should be cleared or closed for the season. There was no uniform moral alignment among them. ## Flourishing under new moons (Years 322–618) As moon-fragment powers became better understood, the Straits of Twin Lanterns became a maritime region notable for thriving trade routes and scholarly lodges; the name describes two prominent physical navigational lights, not two newly invented moons. Ports built combined observation towers and ordinary beacon networks. Some schools used lunar arts for ice warnings and wave sensing while keeping weatherbooks, depth ropes and trained shorewatchers. Merfolk observers exchanged current readings with harbor crews, but underwater polities retained the right to decline surface contracts. The small Sea-Glass College sponsored experimentation in weather prediction, healing, metals and winter navigation. Its high fees excluded fisher households until Master Sivi Redd, a Gnome instrument maker, established an independent public teaching workshop that demonstrated low-cost alternatives. Several wealthy scholars mocked the small instruments; her students successfully predicted a dangerous shoal season using mundane observations in combination with lunar measurements. When the college attempted to acquire the workshop, dockworkers and students kept it independent. This was a victory for access, not proof that every coastal school became generous. ### Giant sky courts and reluctant guests Highland Giant speakers gathered at the Rock-and-Star Moot to debate safe passes and hillside quarrying. Some used renewed magical observation to protect lower villages; others refused cooperation, claiming that newcomers were draining ancient upland resources. A dispute involving a collapsed shelter was resolved by a work levy paid partly by large-house quarry interests rather than forcing poorer valley households to provide unpaid labor. The Moot was one regional political culture, not the government of all Giants. ## The hard peace of the coast (Years 619–960) A short regional conflict known as the War of the Beacon Keys broke out among competing small maritime lordships over ownership of lights, salvage rights and the ability to deny passage. Port militias set fires in warehouses and confiscated winter stores. A partially enchanted beacon failed after being tampered with, and ships wrecked because captains had trusted its signal. The war never involved Orcs, the southern Avarran mage exiles or the global east–west wars of undated later history. The end came through the Harbor Witness Compact, negotiated by rival boatbuilders, Merfolk navigators, some Harpy coastal scouts and grieving fishing families. Its best-known clause prohibited any signatory harbor from deliberately displaying a false safety light, even during war. A few captains obeyed it at enormous personal cost; later rulers broke it. The compact nonetheless became a model for subsequent port laws and a reminder that an agreement can matter even when it fails to end every abuse. Meanwhile, winter medicine developed in inland valleys. A Bearfolk physician, Era Vennpine, organized the Blue-Snow Houses, public huts stocked with dry linen, salted broth and simple medical supplies. Their use of permitted lunar healing was celebrated, but they did not require magical practitioners for every rescue. Some landowners objected to feeding people traveling without permission; several huts were burned in reprisals, then rebuilt from donated timber. No whole species is cast as invariably kind or unkind. ## New prosperity, old divisions (Years 961–1,321) Tharvorn's last centuries in Avarra's “Wonder” date band saw competing northern successes: trade cities enriched by steel, timber and harbor tolls; small coastal settlements sustained by mutual shelter; rich courts commissioning enchanted winter gardens; and miners injured in profitable mountain excavations. A succession crisis in Veskhar Reach, now only one of several rival port powers, exposed how fragile hereditary claims were. A council of merchants tried to replace a disputed child claimant with an oligarchic regime; work crews demanded representation and limited their ability to rule by credit alone. The Harbor Assembly of Eight Benches gave each of several occupational constituencies a place to speak, though it still excluded many people and did not transform every port. The Archive of Lost Crews collected accounts of vanished fishers, guides and prisoners across decades, preserving names of the poor alongside nobles. Unlike impossible First Age archives, its source documents arose in the Second Age itself. Some names were transcribed incorrectly; volunteers kept corrections visible rather than invent false certainty. ### The people beneath the chroniclers' headings Human towns were not all sailor kingdoms; Wolvenkin neighborhoods included scholars, farmers, soldiers and couriers; Bearfolk families varied from solitary homesteaders to busy political households. Troll merchants could be fair or violent. Giant circles disagreed over land and sacrifice. Harpy flights were independent cliff and port communities, not a universal warning corps. Gnome, Goblin and Halfling households built permanent lives in selected areas rather than passing through for other peoples' benefit. Merfolk communities sometimes restricted surface access for good reasons. Drakari visitors, if any in a particular dispute, are not automatically given a role, a named patron or a throne. ## The late Second Age (Years 1,322–1,437) The Frost-Hearth Confederation and Red-Lantern Custom in the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437) represent a later northern rescue tradition, not a rename of the earlier Four Smoke Lodges or Harbor Witness Compact. They can share practical values without being the same continuous institution. The ending global earthquakes harmed places far from their origin, but no precise Tharvorn casualty census or destroyed capital is fixed here. No species went extinct. Tharvorn's own names for these periods are still to be decided.
